Pat Karney had represented Harpurhey for Labour since 1979 and had been well-known as the authority's city centre spokesman. He had been suffering from cancer and had been having treatment at The Christie hospital. Manchester City Council leader Garry Bridges said he was "Manchester through and through and he never lost his determination to champion the city or his astute political judgement". 'Great sense of fun' Bridges said: "Pat was a giant of Manchester politics and one of the city's most recognisable public figures for nearly 50 years. "He never lost his connection to where he came from. He was proud to be from Collyhurst and to represent the people of Harpurhey and Collyhurst." He said that although Karney was "deeply serious about his politics and his values", he also had "a great sense of fun" and was not afraid to use "a gimmick or two" to get his message across. title: Public inquiry over Manchester synagogue attack deaths

input.lead: The Home Secretary confirms a public inquiry will examine Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby's deaths
input.summary: The Home Secretary confirms a public inquiry will examine Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby's deaths
input.evidence_text: Public inquiry over Manchester synagogue attack deaths - BBC News Image source, Family handouts Image caption, Adrian Daulby, left, and Melvin Cravitz, right, were killed in the attack on the synagogue in Manchester By Daniel Wittenberg North West Published 12 October 2026 Updated 13 October 2026 A public inquiry will examine the deaths of two men killed during an attack at a synagogue in Manchester last year. Melvin Cravitz, 66, died from multiple stab wounds and fellow worshipper Adrian Daulby, 53, was killed by a bullet fired by armed police as he blocked the synagogue doors when Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, tried to get in the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue on 2 October 2025. Announcing the inquiry, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said: "What happened that day must be fully understood." Syrian-born UK citizen Al-Shamie was shot dead by police while carrying out the attack. Police had already seized Al-Shamie's mobile phone containing details of his "extremist mindset", but did not analyse the contents until after he had attacked the synagogue. The attack took place on Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the year for Jews. Mahmood said: "In recent days, we marked the first anniversary of the terror attack at the Heaton Park synagogue. "On that awful day in October of last year, as our Jewish community celebrated Yom Kippur, two brave men – Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby – lost their lives, and three others were seriously injured. "What happened that day must be fully understood. "So, as requested by the coroner, I can today announce a public inquiry into the deaths of Mr Cravitz and Mr Daulby. "This will ensure that all evidence can be heard, including any sensitive national security material that could not otherwise be fully heard in the coroner's court." Image sourc

title: Our memorial garden helps us grieve - a cemetery felt too far away

input.lead: Emma Moore shares how creating a special place at home has helped her family
input.summary: Emma Moore shares how creating a special place at home has helped her family
input.evidence_text: Our memorial garden helps us grieve - a cemetery felt too far away - BBC News Image source, Emma Moore Image caption, Emma Moore says the garden has given her family, including elder daughter Penelope, a focus following the death of baby Mabel By George Sandeman Published 14 October 2026, 01:06 BST Updated 19 minutes ago When Emma Moore's daughter Mabel died, visiting her in a cemetery felt too far away. "I don't like going to them and I feel like [visits] fizzle out," she says. "At first, you'll go regularly and then it'll start being once a year." Mabel was born prematurely at 27 weeks in April, her lungs had not fully developed and she lived for just two days. Emma keeps Mabel's ashes next to a photograph of her tiny feet but she wanted a special place to feel close to her. "So we created something in the garden... [to] always be reminded of her every day," she tells Morning Live . The stillness of green spaces "can help us connect with memories" of loved ones, says Andy Langford, clinical director at Cruse Bereavement Support. And there are ways to create a special place of calm to remember anyone you've lost - even if you don't have a garden or know much about plants. Image source, Emma Moore Image caption, Emma, with her partner Louis and daughter Penelope, says the garden reminds them of Mabel each day "I'd never done anything like this before, so I had no clue about where to start," says Emma, 35, who lives near Bolton with her partner Louis and daughter Penelope. She chose to dedicate a part of the garden with a willow tree to Mabel. "I've enjoyed doing the gardening and planting. It was nice to focus on something." Of all the flowers the family have planted in Mabel's garden, Emma's favourite are the lilies. Morning Live - Memorial Gardens Families speak about

input.evidence_text: Councillor Pat Karney Mr Christmas and Manchester's constant cheerleader - farewell to a city legend as Pat Karney dies aged 78 Following the death of Pat Karney, Dianne Bourne remembers two sides of a Manchester legend - the radical 80s politician wh Add to preferred sources News Dianne Bourne Lifestyle Editor 00:20, 14 Oct 2026 Updated 06:27, 14 Oct 2026 It's about as fitting as it gets that the final social media post from Councillor Pat Karney was one celebrating Manchester and Christmas , two of his greatest passions. title: Is the funding market getting harder and what could that mean for Manchester? | Manchester Digital

input.lead: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing.
input.summary: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised
input.evidence_text: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised. More capital is being concentrated in fewer companies while the market for exits remains difficult Financial news recently added another dimension to that discussion. AI-related shares fell last week after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slower approach to the development of increasingly capable AI models. Nvidia finished the day down 3.4%, SoftBank fell 10.7% in Tokyo Additionally, the Bank of England is predicted to increase interest rates later this year, which could affect the North West's tech funding landscape by raising the cost of capital across the board, compressing valuations, pushing investors toward profitability over growth-at-all The British Business Bank's 2026 Small Business Equity Tracker found that equity investment into UK smaller businesses fell 4% to £12.3bn in 2025. Seed deal numbers fell 27% and venture deals fell 13%. AI companies attracted 44% of all investment into smaller businesses while the Beauhurst recorded £14.4bn of UK equity investment across 2,799 deals in the first half of 2026 but three AI companies accounted for 29% of all the capital raised. Those very large rounds can make the overall market look stronger than it feels to businesses raising at seed or Ser Beauhurst's analysis shows that UK equity investment more than doubled between 2017 and 2021 to £32.2bn while annual exits remained at around 400 to 500. An exit takes a median of four years from a funding round

input.summary: Bolton Car Boot Sale is one of the North West's biggest weekly boot sales, held in the hardstanding car park of the Macron Stadium (formerly Reebok), Burnden Way, Horwich, Bolton BL6 6JW. It runs every Sunday from February right through to December, drawing over 300 sellers and t
input.evidence_text: Bolton Car Boot Sale is one of the North West's biggest weekly boot sales, held in the hardstanding car park of the Macron Stadium (formerly Reebok), Burnden Way, Horwich, Bolton BL6 6JW. It runs every Sunday from February right through to December, drawing over 300 sellers and thousands of bargain hunters each week. Sellers can arrive and set up from 6:00 AM, with buyers welcomed in from 7:00 AM. Entry costs just £1 per car for buyers. Pitches for sellers are £14 for a car, £20 for a van and £3 for a trailer, with regular and corner pitches available on request. Bring exact change to keep the queue moving, and call organiser Andrew on 07470784644 for more details. Expect hundreds of stalls across the concrete hardstanding pitches, so it goes ahead in most weather. On-site you'll find a 5-star catering service, doughnuts and coffee, ice cream and desserts, a meat auction, fresh fruit and veg, plants, and retro sweet stalls. The sale is dog-friendly, has male and female toilets, ample parking, and kids' rides and bouncy castles to keep little ones entertained.
